effects.effect: some crystals conduct only along their surface, where nothing scatters the current
two metals joined at different temperatures make a voltage

how: Health patches that track heart rhythm or blood oxygen need recharging every few days, which is when people stop wearing them. The patch turns the small warmth difference between skin and air into current using thin films of bismuth telluride, which is also a topological insulator; shaping it so current runs through its scatter-free surface could raise the output enough to run the sensor nonstop.
obstacle: Whether surface currents really improve heat-to-power conversion at body temperature is still unproven.
searchQuery: topological insulator surface states thermoelectric wearable body heat
why: Body-heat wearables run only tiny loads; the topological boost is only predicted.

name: Air-skin stent
subtitle: a stent blood cannot clot on

effects.effect: microscopic bumps make water bead up and roll off, carrying dirt away
platelets clump to clot blood

how: After a stent props open a heart artery, patients take blood thinners for months or years, which cause dangerous bleeding, because platelets stick to the metal and form clots. A stent coated in microscopic water-repelling bumps holds a thin cushion of air against the blood, so platelets have nothing to cling to.
obstacle: Under blood pressure the trapped air dissolves within hours to days, after which the surface acts like plain metal.
searchQuery: superhydrophobic stent air layer thrombosis in vivo
why: Water-repelling coatings cut clotting in lab tests; no stent keeps its air layer in the body.

name: Quantum-dot brain voltage probe
subtitle: glowing dots that report every neuron's firing

effects.effect: crystals a few nanometres wide glow in a colour set purely by their size
an electric field splits a glowing gas's colour lines
nerve signals are electrical

how: Electrodes in the brain hear only a few hundred neurons each, while a mind-reading interface would want many thousands. Crystal dots a few nanometres wide, slipped into the membranes of nerve cells, change their glow when the cell fires, because an electric field shifts the colour such tiny crystals give off; a fibre-optic camera then reads thousands of neurons at once by their flicker.
obstacle: Getting the dots to sit stably in cell membranes without harming neurons, and doing it in a living human brain.
searchQuery: quantum dot voltage sensor neuron membrane in vivo imaging
why: Membrane dots reported voltage in cultured cells; never used to read a living brain.

name: Microfibre-digesting washer filter
subtitle: a washing machine filter that digests polyester fluff

effects.effect: bacteria found at a recycling plant make an enzyme that breaks PET plastic apart
catalysis

how: Every wash sheds hundreds of thousands of polyester fibres that slip through sewage plants into rivers and seas, and today's lint filters only collect fluff for landfill. This filter traps the fibres on a mesh coated with a heat-hardened version of the PET-eating enzyme, which breaks them back into their harmless building blocks between washes so nothing needs emptying.
obstacle: The enzyme works slowly on tightly packed fibres, and detergents and bleach wear it down.
searchQuery: PETase enzyme washing machine microfiber filter digest
why: Lint filters and PET enzymes exist; nothing digests the fibres where they are caught.

name: Laser-pushed light sail
subtitle: a laser-driven sail to the nearest stars

effects.effect: light pushes on what it hits
tiny repeated structures bend light, sound or radio the 'wrong' way
a laser makes sodium atoms high in the sky glow as an artificial star for correcting blur

how: Even our fastest probes would take tens of thousands of years to reach the nearest star, so no spacecraft has ever visited another solar system. A sail lighter than a postage stamp, patterned so that it reflects the beam and steers itself back to the middle of it, is pushed by a vast array of ground lasers to a fifth of light speed; laser guide stars let the array cancel the air's blur so the beam stays on the sail for minutes.
obstacle: The ground lasers would need hundreds of gigawatts, more than many countries' total power.
searchQuery: laser light sail beam-riding metamaterial sail demonstration
why: Self-steering sail designs tested on the bench; no sail has ever been laser-launched.

name: Self-sealing subsea power cable
subtitle: an offshore power cable that heals its insulation

effects.effect: capsules in a plastic burst when it cracks and glue the crack shut
conduction

how: Offshore wind farms lose more money to failed seabed cables than to anything else, and each repair needs a special ship and weeks of lost power. The cable's insulation holds tiny capsules that burst when water or a scrape opens a crack and fill it with fresh insulating resin before it grows into a short circuit.
obstacle: The healing resin must work cold and under seawater pressure, and match the insulation well enough to stand high voltage.
searchQuery: self-healing insulation subsea power cable microcapsule high voltage
why: Self-healing cable insulation is studied in labs; no subsea cable uses it.

name: Graphene heavy-water separator
subtitle: makes heavy water with far less energy

effects.effect: graphene lets protons through but stops every atom and molecule
a current splits water into hydrogen and oxygen

how: Heavy water, needed for some reactors, for medical scanning tracers and as fuel for future fusion plants, is made today by plants that boil and react vast amounts of water with toxic hydrogen sulphide. A current drives hydrogen nuclei from water through a sheet of graphene, which lets ordinary ones through about ten times faster than heavy ones, so each pass leaves the water richer in heavy hydrogen, with no toxic gas and far less energy.
obstacle: Each pass enriches only a little, so a plant needs many stages of large, flawless graphene that does not yet exist.
searchQuery: graphene membrane deuterium enrichment heavy water production scale
why: Graphene separated hydrogen isotopes in a 2016 lab study; no production unit exists.

name: Skull-lens ultrasound brain scanner
subtitle: a headset that maps brain activity through bone

effects.effect: tiny repeated structures bend light, sound or radio the 'wrong' way
sound echoes

how: Brain scanners that track thought, like fMRI, fill a room, and functional ultrasound, which watches blood rush to busy brain areas, works only through a hole in the skull. A thin cap patterned with tiny structures, shaped from a scan of the wearer's own skull, pre-bends the sound to cancel the bone's distortion, so a headset could map brain activity through intact bone.
obstacle: Bone soaks up most of the high-pitched sound needed for sharp images, leaving very faint echoes.
searchQuery: metasurface skull aberration correction functional ultrasound transcranial human
why: Functional ultrasound needs a skull window today; skull-correcting lenses are only bench tests.
